subject: science
passage: In 1800, the naturalist Alexander von Humboldt described electric eels in a Venezuelan pool rising from the water to press themselves against horses that local fishers had driven in. For nearly two centuries, many biologists treated the account as an exaggeration, since eels were known to deliver their shocks while fully submerged. Experiments in the 2010s, however, showed that an eel confronting a partly submerged threat will indeed leap up and press its chin against it. Out of the water, the current that would otherwise spread into the surrounding water passes instead through the threat's body, so the shock it receives is stronger. The behavior, researchers suggest, may help eels defend themselves when shrinking dry-season pools leave them exposed.
stem: According to the text, why is an eel's shock stronger when the eel leaps up to press against a threat?

choices.A: The eel can generate more electricity when part of its body is exposed to the open air.
choices.B: Shrinking pools in the dry season leave eels more exposed to possible predators.
choices.C: Less current is lost to the surrounding water, so more passes through the threat.
choices.D: The surrounding water carries the eel's current directly into the threat's body.

explanation.why: The fourth sentence explains the mechanism: out of the water, "the current that would otherwise spread into the surrounding water passes instead through the threat's body, so the shock it receives is stronger." The shock is stronger because less current is lost to the water, not because the eel produces more.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says the eel produces more electricity in air; it says the same current is directed through the threat instead of spreading into the water.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the situation in which the behavior may be useful, not the reason the shock is stronger.
explanation.C: Correct. This restates the text's explanation: current that would spread into the water passes through the threat instead.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says the water spreads the current away; leaping out of the water keeps it from doing so.
